subject: Astronomy & Space
title: The Discovery of the Expanding Universe
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Discovery of the Expanding Universe.

hook.text: In 1929, Hubble found that galaxies are flying apart. The farther away, the faster they recede.

buildup.text: By measuring galaxy redshifts, he showed a clear pattern: distance and recession speed are directly proportional.

discovery.text: This meant the universe is expanding—and rewinding implies everything started from a single point.

twist.text: Lemaître actually published the same idea two years earlier in 1927, but his paper was largely ignored at the time.

climax.text: The expanding universe became the foundation of modern cosmology and the strongest evidence for the Big Bang.

punchline.text: Galaxies racing apart in every direction. The universe is still growing.

quiz.question: What pattern did Hubble discover about galaxies?
options: The farther a galaxy, the faster it moves away from us
All galaxies rotate at the same speed
Galaxies move toward a single point in space

details.summary: In 1929, Edwin Hubble combined his galaxy distance measurements with Vesto Slipher's redshift data to show that galaxies are moving away from us, with more distant ones receding faster.
details.whyItMatters: The expanding universe implied that space, time, and matter had a beginning — the Big Bang. This discovery overturned millennia of belief in a static, eternal universe and became the foundation of modern cosmology.
takeaways: Hubble showed galaxies recede faster with greater distance
This proved the universe is expanding, not static
It implied the universe had a beginning — the Big Bang

faq.question: Did Einstein predict the expanding universe?
faq.answer: His general relativity equations naturally implied it, but Einstein added a 'cosmological constant' to force a static universe — believing it had to be eternal.

faq.question: Who really deserves credit for discovering the expanding universe?
faq.answer: Lemaître published the relationship between distance and recession velocity in 1927, two years before Hubble. Slipher measured the redshifts Hubble used. Hubble contributed the crucial distance measurements. The 2018 renaming to the Hubble-Lemaître Law partially addresses this shared credit.
